new_statements.relation_note: Catalog StressTyp2 record for Cakchiquel is final stress = fixed final stress; Townsend states exactly that (accent always on the last syllable), adding only the Spanish-loan exemption and an observation that stress shifts rightward onto added suffix syllables. Variety described: San Juan Comalapa (Chimaltenango, Guatemala), stated to be readily understood from Solola to San Juan Sacatepequez.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is invariably on the final syllable of native Cakchiquel words; when a suffix adds a syllable the stress moves off the root onto the new final syllable (with attendant root-vowel change e -> a in one verb class).
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loanwords are exempt from the final-accent rule (they keep their Spanish accent). No other exceptions given.
new_statements.identity_note: Townsend's grammar is explicitly based on the Cakchiquel of San Juan Comalapa, Department of Chimaltenango, Guatemala (Introduction para. 1, p. 9), which he says is readily understood from Solola to San Juan Sacatepequez 'but each town varies somewhat'. The orthography is Spanish-based (pre-ALMG); the work is a 1926 manuscript published in 1961 as a historical document with a foreword by K. L. Pike.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict' final stress (final stress) is correct: the Berinstein 1979 quotations are verbatim at pp. vi, 47, 52 of the eScholarship scan (now saved to our files; previously only a /tmp copy existed), and the held 1997 OKMA reference grammar (Rukemik ri Kaqchikel Chi', pp. 20-21, sec. 'Acento') states the same rule explicitly for radical, derived and compound words with directional enclitics attracting the stress, as do the held Bennett 2016 (p.495), Bennett 2018 (fn.7: word-final, no secondary stress) and ALMG 2004, and the newly downloaded Nelson 2020 acoustic check. No source contradicts. The weakness is only in the pin: the record's deciding citation is a 1979 perception thesis reached through StressTyp2/Gordon 2002, with empty quote/cite/grade fields on the main record, while a native-speaker reference grammar we already hold gives the rule first-hand. Action: re-pin

sources.quote: 'The preceding examples show that Kaqchikel does in fact place main word stress on the final syllable of the word. However, there are a few exceptions ... Word-final stress is by far the most common pattern for native vocabulary' -- janila /xanila/ 'very' has penultimate stress (Fig. 6); Spanish loans variable (ruxumprente); 'while Kaqchikel overwhelmingly prefers word-final stress, there is no absolute restriction against other patterns.'
sources.locator: sec. 3.1 'Word stress', pp. 75-77 (acoustic examples, 1-4 syllable words, Figs. 2-7)
sources.note: Only acoustic verification of Kaqchikel word-final stress found (pitch/intensity tracks on 1-4 syllable words); documents the janila and loanword exceptions instrumentally.
